chapter: Trio, Eckstine accompanist and Illinois Jacquet, 1945-48
title: J.J. Johnson's trombone concept in the Jacquet band
summary: Johnson plays fast, articulate lines with a short slide, drawing questions from symphony players.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: Oh, I forgot to mention the other person in the band that was very significant. I don't know how I missed him. It was J.J. Johnson. I kept thinking back, counting the people that I named. I named Leo Parker and Illinois, of course, and Joe Newman, and Illinois' brother, Russell, and of course, the three men in the rhythm section, and all the while I was thinking there had to be somebody else.

And that other person was another real spark in the band, J.J. Johnson, who was really... He was young and into his... To me, he was at his peak of playing. And he was playing like non one else then. There are trombone players since then who seem to have caught on to his method, and a lot of them have became very proficient in it. But at that particular time, no one was playing trombone like J.J. Johnson. In talking to him and talking to other trombone players, he had gotten a whole new concept of playing. I don't know whether he ever wrote any books on this or what. But whatever we played in some of the big halls that we played around, where the symphony orchestras played, there was always some of the players who
played in the symphony orchestras around J.J. talking to him about the way he played.

And the way he played was that he played very fast, he was very articulate, and his slide never went over 6 inches out from his mouthpiece. And how this happened... I don't know how to play trombone, but obviously it had to be something to do with the way he manipulated the sound from his mouth -- you know, his chops.

But in talking to him about this, he was saying that in some ways, you couldn't play like that when you were playing with a section, because technically, there are certain sounds that you had to... I guess like violinists bowing, you had to use the slide a different way. All of this a trombone player would understand.

But it was really an experience working with him, because I never heard a trombone player play like that, and play that fast and with that much articulation -- and he really knew what he was doing, you know! He was also an excellent arranger, you know.
